title: The Mongols become Muslim
hook: within decades, Mongol rulers in Persia embrace Islam

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ain Jalut, where the Mamluks stopped the Mongol advance, beside a spring named for Goliath. Your line was: the spring of goliath. Did you stay on your line when it was tested? Day nine hundred sixty-one.

A Mongol prince stands in front of a gathering and takes a new name: Mahmud. His name until then was Ghazan. He is a descendant of Chinggis Khan, and he is reaching for the throne of Persia, the land his family's armies once overran. Rashid al-Din, who would serve him as vizier and write the history of the Mongols, describes him as raised a Buddhist. And now he declares himself a Muslim. Same family. Same throne. An heir of the storm from the east, praying toward Mecca. Today's words: the Mongols become Muslim.
screen: `A PRINCE TAKES A NEW NAME.` → `GHAZAN BECOMES MAHMUD.` → `THE STORM'S HEIR PRAYS.`

segments.voice: It wasn't only Ghazan. In the north, Berke, khan of the Golden Horde, had become Muslim before him. In Persia, after Ghazan, the Mongol rulers were Muslims, and they built mosques, endowed schools and gave scholars their patronage. The family whose armies had sacked Baghdad now ruled as Muslim kings. Hence the line: the conquerors converted. Here the people who won the war took up the faith of the people they had defeated. Why did it happen? Historians weigh it differently. Some stress faith, the plain story Rashid al-Din tells of a ruler who came to believe. Some stress politics: a king ruling a land full of mosques does well to pray in them. Some point to the scholars, Sufis and ordinary people around the court, whose lives showed the conquerors what Islam looked like. It's probably more than one of these at once. People are like that. And here's how the tradition itself talks about a change of heart. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that the hearts of people are between two of the fingers of the Most Merciful, and He turns them as He wills. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, another report says, often prayed asking the turner of hearts to keep his heart firm. Some tell this story as a reminder that no one's ending is known in advance.
screen: `BERKE IN THE NORTH, GHAZAN IN PERSIA.` · `THE WINNERS TOOK THE FAITH OF THE LOSERS.` · `FAITH, POLITICS, OR PEOPLE?` · `HEARTS BETWEEN TWO FINGERS.` · then, large: `THE CONQUERORS CONVERTED.`

segments.voice: The practice: believe change is possible. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've quietly written off. A relative who will never change. A colleague you've filed under impossible. Or yourself, in one stubborn area. Hold them in mind without arguing for or against. Then ask yourself honestly: is the ending written yet? If you pray, you can ask Allah, the turner of hearts, to turn that heart, or yours, toward good. If you don't, simply leave the door in your mind open a crack, and let them stand in it. The bell holds the time.
The Mongols become Muslim. The rulers whose armies had swept through Persia and sacked Baghdad, taking up Islam, like Ghazan, who became Mahmud. Today's words.
Your line: the conquerors converted. Today, treat the person you'd written off as if their story isn't finished: one kind word, one fresh chance. Day nine hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Muslims tell the conversion of the Mongol rulers as a story of hearts turned, and the Prophet's prayer to the turner of hearts, asking for a heart kept firm in faith, is still said by Muslims today.

fork.setup: you're Ghazan, a Mongol prince raised a Buddhist, ruling Persia, a land full of mosques. what do you do?
options: keep the religion you were raised in.
become Muslim and take a new name.
rule with no religion at all.
fork.reveal: Rashid al-Din says he declared himself a Muslim and took the name Mahmud. the conquerors converted.

trapdoor: what you thought: conquerors make the conquered take their religion.
what it means: here the conquerors took up the faith of the people they had conquered: Ghazan, raised a Buddhist, became Mahmud.
what a scholar hears: Rashid al-Din's Jami' al-Tawarikh, Berke of the Golden Horde before Ghazan, and a live debate about faith and politics in conversion.

sources.ref: Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh (Ghazan's upbringing and conversion)
Sahih Muslim 2654 (hearts between two fingers of the Most Merciful)

notes: No dates or 'within decades' timing given, under the claims rule (the index hook says 'within decades').
Ghazan's Buddhist upbringing, conversion and the name Mahmud are paraphrased from Rashid al-Din; confirm.
Berke of the Golden Horde converting before Ghazan: standard history; confirm wording 'in the north'.
'After Ghazan, the Mongol rulers [in Persia] were Muslims': confirm (Öljeitü and Abu Sa'id).
Sahih Muslim 2654 and Tirmidhi 2140 paraphrased; confirm numbering. Tirmidhi's report says the Prophet often prayed with these words; the script says 'often prayed', as the report does. Confirm.

Editor: Ghazan converted before taking the throne, so the hook now says he is reaching for it, and Rashid al-Din is his future vizier; the garbled closing 'proof that the ending isn't written until it is' became an attributed, softer line.
Audit (y3 957-966): checked Ghazan/Berke history and hadith references; no change needed. Note: Tekuder (Ahmad) was a Muslim Ilkhan before Ghazan; the script does not claim otherwise.
